title: The luminous mysteries
hookLine: added by John Paul II in 2002: baptism, Cana, the kingdom, transfiguration, Eucharist (Thursdays)

cards: Picture the whole Gospel laid out on a table, and the rosary's mysteries as pins stuck into it. For a long time there were fifteen. Five joyful: the birth and childhood of Jesus.
Five sorrowful: his suffering and death. Five glorious: the resurrection and after. There's a big empty stretch in the middle.
Jesus is twelve in the Temple, and the very next pin is the night before he dies. Everything in between, the baptism, the miracles, the parables, the crowds, is missing.
Then in October 2002, a pope who had prayed the rosary since he was young added five.

teach.b: Pope John Paul the Second called them the mysteries of light, in Latin mysteria lucis. Luminous means full of light.

Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "I am the light of the world: he that followeth me, walketh not in darkness, but shall have the light of life." These five cover his public life, when that light was out in the open.
First, the Baptism in the Jordan: Jesus goes down into the water, the heavens open, and a voice calls him the beloved Son.
Second, the Wedding at Cana: the wine runs out, and Mary tells the servants, in the Douay-Rheims: "Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye." Water becomes wine, his first sign.
Third, the Proclamation of the Kingdom: the preaching, the call to turn around, the forgiveness.

Fourth, the Transfiguration: on a mountain, his face shines like the sun in front of three friends. Fifth, the Institution of the Eucharist: the Last Supper, the bread and cup you met at the consecration last week.

The baptism, Cana and the mountain were all stories in Camp Two; now they're beads. The Pope suggested praying them on Thursdays, the day of the Last Supper, and moved the joyful mysteries to Saturday to make room.
He said plainly the addition was offered freely, not imposed. Some Catholics pray all twenty. Some keep the traditional fifteen.
Both are at home in the Church.

teach.h: I AM THE LIGHT OF THE WORLD.
teach.b: The gap is filled: the rosary now walks through the whole life, including the years when the light was out on the road.

how: Catholics who use them pray the luminous mysteries of the rosary on Thursdays, meditating on the Baptism of Jesus, the Wedding at Cana, the Proclamation of the Kingdom, the Transfiguration and the Institution of the Eucharist; some keep the traditional fifteen mysteries.

o: a set of hymns sung at a wedding
prayers said by candlelight at Easter
five rosary scenes from Jesus's public life

games.q: match each luminous mystery — tap the pairs.
p: the heavens open over the Jordan
whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye
his face shines on a mountain

s: the luminous mysteries are as old as the rosary
John Paul the Second added them in October 2002.
they fill the gap between Jesus's childhood and his passion
the fifteen traditional mysteries skipped his public life. these five fill it.
every Catholic is required to pray the luminous mysteries
the Pope offered them freely. some pray all twenty; some keep the traditional fifteen.

games.q: you're a servant at a wedding in Cana. the wine has run out. Jesus's mother turns to you. what does she say?
o: whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye.
tell the guests the feast is over.
games.why: "Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye." he tells you to fill the jars with water, and it becomes wine: his first sign.

practice: Pick one scene, the river, the wedding running out of wine, the crowds, the mountain, the supper, and put yourself inside it; at Cana, maybe you're a servant, told to fill jars with water and not sure why.
If you pray, begin a luminous decade on your fingers, and let the scene play. If you don't, stay with the picture, and notice where the light falls.

wordCard.voice: Luminous mysteries. Five scenes of light from Jesus's public life, added to the rosary in 2002 and prayed on Thursdays. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: mysteries of light, John Paul the Second's name for the luminous mysteries.

carryVoice: Your line: the light years. Thursday now has five scenes of its own. That's day one hundred twenty.
